question.problem: Given that the function $f(x)={x}^{5}+3{x}^{2}-x$ has a critical point in the interval $[0,1],$ use the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting from ${x}_{0}=0.5$ to estimate the critical point. Round your final answer to two decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{5}+3{x}^{2}-x)^{′}=5{x}^{4}+6x-1, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(5{x}^{4}+6x-1)^{′}=20{x}^{3}+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{5{x}_{n}^{4}+6{x}_{n}-1}{20{x}_{n}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(20{x}_{n}^{3}+6)-(5{x}_{n}^{4}+6{x}_{n}-1)}{20{x}_{n}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15{x}_{n}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{n}^{3}+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{15{x}_{0}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{0}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15(0.5)^{4}+1}{20(0.5)^{3}+6} \\  & =0.227\,941….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{15{x}_{1}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{1}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15(0.227\,941…)^{4}+1}{20(0.227\,941…)^{3}+6} \\  & =0.166\,829…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{15{x}_{2}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{2}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15(0.166\,829…)^{4}+1}{20(0.166\,829…)^{3}+6} \\  & =0.166\,033….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{2}≈0.17$ and ${x}_{3}≈0.17$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈0.17,$ rounded to two decimal places.
